answer_text:
We want an integer \(z\) such that

\[
(n+1)z \equiv 1 \pmod{n^2}.
\]

Consider the product

\[
(n+1)(1-n).
\]

Expanding,

\[
(n+1)(1-n)=n+1-n^2-n=1-n^2.
\]

Since \(1-n^2\) differs from \(1\) by a multiple of \(n^2\),

\[
(n+1)(1-n) \equiv 1 \pmod{n^2}.
\]

Thus

\[
z \equiv 1-n \pmod{n^2}.
\]

The least positive representative of this congruence is

\[
z = 1-n+n^2 = n^2-n+1.
\]

Therefore, the multiplicative inverse of \(n+1\) modulo \(n^2\) is

\[
\boxed{n^2-n+1}.
\]
